title: Microservices vs Monolith Architecture in 2026 ⚡ (REST vs GraphQL)
ig_caption:
Microservices vs Monolith Architecture in 2026 ⚡ REST vs GraphQL: ask once, waste less.
Same screen: user + posts + likes—watch how APIs differ.

• REST: /user, /posts, /likes → you “ask” multiple times (N+1 vibes)
• Over-fetching: endpoints return extra data you don’t need
• Under-fetching: you end up calling again to fill gaps

• GraphQL: /graphql → one query for exactly the fields required
• Fewer round trips: “REST asks many times; GraphQL asks once”
• Client-driven shape: compose results per UI needs
• Server control: use resolvers + batching to keep it fast

Practical takeaway: For interviews and production, describe the real bottleneck—round trips, payload size, and resolver/database batching—not just “schema vs endpoints.”

Debate question: Which would you bet on for microservices in 2026—REST with smart aggregation, or GraphQL with disciplined resolver performance?

fb_caption:
Microservices vs Monolith Architecture in 2026 ⚡ — REST vs GraphQL is a practical trade-off you’ll feel in microservice-heavy systems.

Scenario: one screen needs a user, their posts, and their likes.

REST approach:
- Call multiple endpoints (e.g., /user, /posts, /likes)
- Typical pain points:
  • More round trips (latency compounds)
  • Over-fetching (payload includes unused fields)
  • Under-fetching (you re-call to fill missing data)
- In production, teams often introduce a backend-for-frontend (BFF) or API gateway aggregation layer to reduce chatter.

GraphQL approach:
- Single endpoint (/graphql) with one query that requests exactly the fields needed by the UI.
- Benefits:
  • “Ask once” reduces network chatter for composed views
  • Better control of response shape per client
- Production lessons:
  • Resolver design matters: avoid classic N+1 database queries
  • Use batching/caching patterns (e.g., DataLoader-style) and strict query complexity limits
  • Apply authentication/authorization at the field level when needed

Architecture guidance (how to choose in 2026):
- If your system already has strong API composition (BFF/gateway), REST can stay clean and fast.
- If your product is UI-driven with many different client shapes, GraphQL can reduce over/under-fetching.
- Regardless of choice: measure p95 latency, payload size, query counts, and resolver/db fan-out.
